¶ 6. The apparent sense, ‘until now I thought the celandine was blue’, must be misleading; it is
not credible that S., who, according to Mary S., ‘knew every plant by its name’ (1824 Preface), did
not know that the celandine is yellow. The intended sense is possibly that S. associated the celandine
with Wordsworth, just as he associated a blue flower with another writer. Perhaps Rousseau was in S.’s
mind; the periwinkle was ‘The flower which Rousseau brought into such fashion among the Parisians,
by exclaiming one day, “Ah, voilà de la pervenche!” ’ (Moore’s note to The Fudge Family in Paris (1818)
Letter xii line 72). The incident itself is in R.’s Confessions (1781) Bk VI. A less likely possibility is that
S.’s reference is to the gentian, and that its association for him was with Coleridge; cp. C.’s note to his

absence of a first draft could imply indoor composition, while Mary S. seems uncertain when
